Text incipit: In dich hab ich gehoffet, Herr; hilf, daß ich nicht zu schanden werd
Melodic incipit: D4 D4 A4 E4 G4 F4 E4 D4 D4 A4 B4 C5 B4 A4 G#4 A4
Later sources: Wolff 1569; Nürnberg 1571; Stettin 1576; Zinckeisen 1584; Basel 1581; Lauterbach 1585; Neustadt 1586; Leipzig, Kleinod 1591; Greifswalde 1592; Raselius 1599 etc.; Stockholm 1873; Helsingfors 1888
Notes: New section: Jambisch 8.8.7.4.4.7. Vierf. M.; D Dorian; no time signature. To the text "Christus ist erstanden" in a setting by Finck 1536 Nr. 1, and in art settings by Senfl, Bruck and Mahu in Rhaw 1544. In a 15th-c. MS (Royal Library Berlin) with the Easter song "Christ, der ist erstanden"; adapted to "Jesus ist ein süßer Nam" in a Munich MS of 1478. Triller 1555 calls it an old common melody and prints it (p.108, ¢) to "Erstanden ist uns Jesus Christ" ending "Halleluja! Kyrieleison". Osiander 1586 adapted it to "Jesus Christus unser Heiland, der den Tod"; a Nürnberg broadside (ca. 1540) to S. Heyden's "Christus Gottes Sohn unser Herr" (8.8.8.8.4); Artomius 1601 heads it "Christus jam surrexit". Spread with "In dich hab ich gehoffet, Herr" after Straßburg 1560 and with other hymns of this metre (e.g. "Erhör mich, wenn ich ruf zu dir"). Original text probably the Easter song "Christus jam surrexit".

Bach formed his melody from lines 1-4, 10, 11, followed by all Saxon books (Doles, Hiller, Schicht, Hentschel etc.); (10) reworking in Recueil de musique, Strasbourg 1758 S. 38 (Dopp. M.), Straßburg 1809, Stern 1869 (printed, Eb major). Later sources: Köpphl 1537. 45; Schumann 1539; Zürich 1540; Magdeburg 1540; Klug 1543; Babst 1545 etc.; Spangenberg 1545; Walter 1551; in all Protestant hymnals, melody and chorale books to the present; Stockholm 1853; Christiania 1875; Philadelphia 1875; Helsingfors 1888; original form restored after Layriz 1839, Tucher 1848, Bayern 1854 etc., e.g. Brunn 1857, Ritter 1859, Lützel 1859, Wackernagel 1860, Lohmeyer 1861, Anding 1868, Jakob-Richter 1873, Ihme 1873. 88, Hermannsburg 1876, Großherzogtum Hessen 1888, Hessen-Cassel 1890

Notes: Luther's German Te Deum for two choirs in chant notation (breves and semibreves), ending with Amen. Already in Klug 1535, Bl. 56b with variants (semibreves at *, variants 1)-4) printed); probably already in the lost Klug GB of 1529. Simplification of the melismatic pre-Reformation Latin melody, which appears with prose German translation in Breslau 1525, Erfurt 1525, Enchiridion Erfurt 1526, Zwickau 1528, Weisse 1531 and Bohemian Brethren books 1566-1639. In the Rationalist era a watered-down text or Klopstock's adaptation was underlaid and the melody weakened by passing notes. Zahn adds newer melodies for comparison (8653 ff.). Pitches approximate; final not read. Starts p.328, ends p.330.
